nodes.section: Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Over an algebraically closed field of odd characteristic, an indecomposable self-injective cellular algebra of polynomial growth is Morita equivalent to one of the listed symmetric algebras (1)-(7).

nodes.name: Cellular algebra
nodes.statement:
An associative algebra $A$ over a field $K$ is called a \emph{cellular algebra} with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$ 
if the following conditions are satisfied: 
\begin{description}
\item[(C1)] 
$\varLambda$ is a finite partially ordered set with a partial order $\geq$.  
For each $\lambda \in \varLambda$, there exists a finite set $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ such that
the algebra $A$ has a $K$-basis 
\begin{align*} 
\mathcal{C} =\{c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \mid \mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda), \, \lambda \in \varLambda\}. 
\end{align*}

\item[(C2)] 
The linear map $\iota : A \rightarrow A$ which sends $c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda}$ to $c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak s}^{\lambda}$ ($\mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$, $\lambda \in \varLambda$) 
gives an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$. 
(Clearly, $\iota$ is an involution.)

\item[(C3)] 
For any $\lambda \in \varLambda$, $\mathfrak s \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ and $a \in A$, there exist $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} \in K$ ($\mathfrak u\in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)$) such that 
\begin{align}

a c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \equiv \sum_{\mathfrak u \in\mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak u \mathfrak t}^{\lambda} \mod A^{>\lambda}, 
\end{align}
where $A^{> \lambda}$ is a subspace of $A$ spanned by 
$\{ c_{\mathfrak s' \mathfrak t'}^{\lambda'} \mid \mathfrak s', \mathfrak t' \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda'), \,  \lambda' > \lambda, \lambda' \in \varLambda\}$, 
and $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a,\mathfrak s)}$ does not depend on $\mathfrak t$. 
\end{description}
The above basis $\mathcal{C}$ is called a \emph{cellular basis}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: An algebra with a basis $c^\lambda_{st}$ indexed by a poset, an anti-involution swapping $s,t$, and a triangular multiplication rule modulo $A^{>\lambda}$.

nodes.name: Right multiplication rule for cellular basis
nodes.statement: c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak s}^{\lambda} a \equiv \sum_{\mathfrak u \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(\iota(a), \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak t \mathfrak u}^{\lambda} \mod A^{>\lambda}.

nodes.statement_short: Applying the anti-involution to (C3) gives the right action rule.

nodes.name: Cell module $\Delta(\lambda)$
nodes.statement:
For each $\lambda \in \varLambda$,  
let $\Delta(\lambda)$ be a $K$-vector space with a basis $\{c_{\mathfrak s}^{\lambda} \mid \mathfrak s \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)\}$. 
We can define an action of $A$ on $\Delta(\lambda)$ by 
\begin{align*}
a \cdot c_{\mathfrak s}^{\lambda} = \sum_{\mathfrak u \in \mathcal{T}(\lambda)} r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} c_{\mathfrak u}^{\lambda}, 
\end{align*}
where $r_{\mathfrak u}^{(a, \mathfrak s)} \in K$ are those coefficients given in \eqref{C a cst}. 
We call the $A$-modules $\Delta(\lambda)$ ($\lambda \in \varLambda$) \emph{cell modules}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta(\lambda)$ has basis $c^\lambda_s$ with $A$ acting by the structure constants of (C3).

nodes.name: Radical of the cell form

nodes.name: Radical of the cell form is a submodule

nodes.name: Simple heads $L(\lambda)$ and the set $\varLambda^+$
nodes.statement:
Put $L(\lambda) = \Delta(\lambda) / \operatorname{rad}_{\langle \,,\, \rangle} \Delta(\lambda)$, 
and $ \varLambda^+ = \{\lambda \in \varLambda \mid L(\lambda) \not=0\}$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Simple modules of a cellular algebra
nodes.statement:
\ 

\begin{enumerate}
\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $L(\lambda)$ is absolutely irreducible. 

\item 
The set $\{L(\lambda) \mid \lambda \in \varLambda^+\}$ is a complete set of representatives of isomorphism classes of simple $A$-modules. 

\item 
For $\lambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+$, we have 
$\dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\lambda), L(\mu)) = \dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\mu), L(\lambda))$ for all $i \geq 0$. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: The $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in\varLambda^+$, are the absolutely irreducible simples, and Ext-dimensions between simples are symmetric.
conclusions: For $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $L(\lambda)$ is absolutely irreducible.
The set $\{L(\lambda) \mid \lambda \in \varLambda^+\}$ is a complete set of representatives of isomorphism classes of simple $A$-modules.
$\dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\lambda), L(\mu)) = \dim_K \operatorname{Ext}_{A}^i (L(\mu), L(\lambda))$ for all $i \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Every arrow of the Gabriel quiver of a cellular algebra has an inverse arrow
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: a cellular algebra $A$ has the bounded quiver presentation $KQ_A/I$ for the Gabriel quiver $Q_A$ of $A$ and an admissible ideal $I$
conclusions: each arrow of $Q_A$ must have the inverse arrow.

nodes.name: Rewriting non-admissible presentations
nodes.statement:
We note that the five classes of algebras we will consider in \S3 are 
defined in the form $KQ/I$ but $I$ are not admissible in the first place, so that we must rewrite them when we apply Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}(iii).
However, in our application, we will see that the rewriting is merely deletion of the loops in the quiver $Q$ which come from vertices of valency 
one in Brauer graphs we start with.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: The algebras of Section 4 are given by non-admissible ideals; rewriting just deletes loops at valency-one vertices.

nodes.name: Branch criterion for cellular Brauer-graph type algebras
nodes.statement:
Hence, Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}(iii) implies that if one of the algebras we consider in \S3 is cellular, then 
either there is no branch in the Brauer graph or 
there is one loop and the endpoint of the loop is the only branch in the Brauer graph whose valency at most four.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: A cellular algebra of the Section 4 classes has a Brauer graph with no branch, or one loop whose endpoint is the only branch.
assumptions: one of the algebras we consider in \S3 is cellular
conclusions: either there is no branch in the Brauer graph or there is one loop and the endpoint of the loop is the only branch in the Brauer graph whose valency at most four.

nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Decomposition matrix $\mathbf D$
nodes.statement: Put $\mathbf D=(d_{\lambda \mu})_{\lambda \in \varLambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+}$, and we call it the \emph{decomposition matrix}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Projective cover $P(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: For $\lambda\in \varLambda^+$, let $P(\lambda)$ be the projective cover of $L(\lambda)$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Cartan matrix $\mathbf C$
nodes.statement:
Let $c_{\lambda\mu} = [P(\lambda) : L(\mu)]$, for $\lambda, \mu \in \varLambda^+$, and put $\mathbf C =(c_{\lambda \mu})_{\lambda,\mu \in \varLambda^+}$. 
Then $\mathbf C$ is the \emph{Cartan matrix} of $A$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Enumeration of $\varLambda$ along a linear extension
nodes.statement:
First, 
we enumerate the elements of $\varLambda$ as $\{\mu_1,\mu_2,\dots \}$ following a chosen linear extension. Hence $i < j$ if $\mu_i < \mu_j$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Subspaces $A(\mu_i)$
nodes.statement:
Next,
let $A(\mu_i)$ be the subspace of $A$ spanned by $\{c_{\mathfrak s \mathfrak t}^{\mu_k} \mid \mathfrak s, \mathfrak t \in \mathcal{T}(\mu_k), \, k \geq i\}$, for $\mu_i \in \varLambda$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: The $A(\mu_i)$ are two-sided ideals
nodes.statement: Then $A(\mu_i)$, for $1\le i \le |\varLambda|$, where $|\varLambda|$ is the size of $\varLambda$, is a two-sided ideal of $A$ by \eqref{C a cst} and \eqref{C cts a}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
conclusions: is a two-sided ideal of $A$

nodes.name: Chain of cell ideals
nodes.statement: A= A(\mu_1) \supset A(\mu_2) \supset \dots \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|}) \supset A(\mu_{|\varLambda|+1})=0.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C seq A

nodes.name: Filtration $P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}$ of a projective cover
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Tensoring the chain of cell ideals with $P(\lambda)$ gives the filtration $P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}$.

nodes.name: Filtration of $P(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: P(\lambda) = P(\lambda)_{\mu_1} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_2} \supset \dots \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}} \supset P(\lambda)_{\mu_{|\varLambda|}+1}=0,
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.label: C seq Pla

nodes.name: Decomposition matrix properties ($\mathbf C=\mathbf D^T\mathbf D$)
nodes.statement:
\ 

\begin{enumerate} 
\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda$ and $\mu \in \varLambda^+$, 
if $d_{\lambda\mu} \not=0$, then we have $\lambda \geq \mu$. 
Moreover, if $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, we have $d_{\lambda \lambda} =1$. 

\item 
For $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$ and the $A$-submodules $P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}$ in the sequence \eqref{C seq Pla}, we have 
$P(\lambda)_{\mu_i}/ P(\lambda)_{\mu_{i+1}} \cong \Delta(\mu_i)^{\oplus d_{\mu_i \lambda}}$ 
as $A$-modules. 

\item 
We have 
$\mathbf C= \mathbf D^T \mathbf D$, where $\mathbf D^T$ is the transpose of $\mathbf D$. 

\item 
We have $\det \mathbf C >0$. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf D$ is unitriangular, $P(\lambda)$ has a cell filtration with multiplicities $d_{\mu\lambda}$, $\mathbf C=\mathbf D^T\mathbf D$ and $\det\mathbf C>0$.
conclusions: if $d_{\lambda\mu} \not=0$, then we have $\lambda \geq \mu$.
We have $\mathbf C= \mathbf D^T \mathbf D$, where $\mathbf D^T$ is the transpose of $\mathbf D$.
We have $\det \mathbf C >0$.
nodes.label: C Prop decom matrix

nodes.name: Morita invariance of cellularity and weak symmetry
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$. 
Then we have the following. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item
If $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$ then the basic algebra $B$ of $A$ is also cellular and 
there is a Morita equivalence between $A$ and $B$ which respects the cellular structure.

\item 
If $A$ is self-injective then $A$ is weakly symmetric. 

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: In characteristic $\ne2$ the basic algebra of a cellular algebra is cellular, and self-injective cellular algebras are weakly symmetric.
assumptions: $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$
conclusions: If $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$ then the basic algebra $B$ of $A$ is also cellular and there is a Morita equivalence between $A$ and $B$ which respects the cellular structure.
If $A$ is self-injective then $A$ is weakly symmetric.
nodes.label: C Prop Morita equiv

nodes.name: Reduction to basic algebras
nodes.statement:
Thanks to Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}), 
it is enough to consider basic algebras in order to determine Morita equivalence classes of cellular algebras  
if the characteristic of the base field is odd.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Endomorphism algebras of projectives are cellular
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field $K$ of odd characteristic. If $P$ is a finitely generated projective $A$-module, 
then $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field $K$ of odd characteristic
conclusions: $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.label: C Lem idem

nodes.name: Proof sketch of Lemma (endomorphism algebras)
nodes.statement:
For the proof, let $Q$ be the direct sum of pairwise inequivalent indecomposable projective $A$-modules that appear 
as direct summands of $P$. Then the opposite algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is of the form $eAe$, for an idempotent $e\in A$. 
We may prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra. As $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is the basic algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$, we have the isomorphism of algebras
$\operatorname{End}_A(P)\cong fM_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))f$, for an idempotent $f$ of the matrix algebra $M_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))$. 
Noting that a matrix algebra over a cellular algebra is a cellular algebra, we deduce that $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra by the same argument 
which we used to prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the basic algebra $eAe$ of $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$, then pass to $fM_n(\cdot)f$ using that matrix algebras over cellular algebras are cellular.

nodes.name: Basic algebra $eAe$
nodes.statement:
For the proof, let $Q$ be the direct sum of pairwise inequivalent indecomposable projective $A$-modules that appear 
as direct summands of $P$. Then the opposite algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is of the form $eAe$, for an idempotent $e\in A$. 
We may prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Matrix form
nodes.statement:
As $\operatorname{End}_A(Q)$ is the basic algebra of $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$, we have the isomorphism of algebras
$\operatorname{End}_A(P)\cong fM_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))f$, for an idempotent $f$ of the matrix algebra $M_n(\operatorname{End}_A(Q))$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement:
Noting that a matrix algebra over a cellular algebra is a cellular algebra, we deduce that $\operatorname{End}_A(P)$ is a cellular algebra by the same argument 
which we used to prove that $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Matrix algebras over cellular algebras are cellular.

nodes.name: Idempotent truncations of cellular algebras are cellular
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field of odd characteristic, then $e A e$ is a cellular algebra for any idempotent $e \in A$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ is a cellular algebra over a field of odd characteristic
conclusions: $e A e$ is a cellular algebra for any idempotent $e \in A$.

nodes.name: Cellularity transfers from a Morita-equivalent corner
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a finite dimensional algebra over a field of odd characteristic, 
and suppose that $eAe$, for an idempotent $e \in A$, and $A$ are Morita equivalent. 
Then, $A$ is a cellular algebra if $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
assumptions: $A$ be a finite dimensional algebra over a field of odd characteristic
suppose that $eAe$, for an idempotent $e \in A$, and $A$ are Morita equivalent.
conclusions: $A$ is a cellular algebra if $eAe$ is a cellular algebra.

nodes.name: Cellularity is determined by the basic algebra
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$ and let $A$ be a finite dimensional $K$-algebra. Then, $A$ is a cellular algebra if and only if 
its basic algebra is a cellular algebra.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
conclusions: $A$ is a cellular algebra if and only if its basic algebra is a cellular algebra.

nodes.name: Proof of consequence (b)
nodes.statement:
For the second statement, we recall that the functor $F:=eA\otimes_A-$ induces 
the equivalence and $Ae\otimes_{eAe}eA\cong A$ holds. Thus, $eA=F(A)$ is a finitely generated projective $eAe$-module and 
$\operatorname{End}_{eAe}(eA)\cong \operatorname{End}_A(A)\cong A^{\rm op}$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Realise $A$ as $\operatorname{End}_{eAe}(eA)^{\rm op}$ with $eA$ projective over $eAe$ and apply the lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of consequence (c)
nodes.statement: The third statement follows from Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}) and (b).
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Combine Morita invariance of cellularity with (b).

nodes.name: Minimal and maximal cell indices
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$ with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$. 
Then we have the following. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is minimal, 
then $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $d_{\lambda \lambda }=1$ and $d_{\lambda \mu}=0$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{\lambda\}$. 

\item 
Assume that $A$ is self-injective. 
If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is maximal, 
then there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that 
$d_{\lambda \mu}=1$ and $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \mu\}$. 
In particular, if $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$ then $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \lambda\}$.

\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Minimal cell indices give unit rows of $\mathbf D$; for self-injective $A$, maximal ones also give rows with a single entry $1$.
assumptions: $A$ be a cellular algebra over a field $K$ with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$
conclusions: If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is minimal, then $\lambda \in \varLambda^+$, $d_{\lambda \lambda }=1$ and $d_{\lambda \mu}=0$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{\lambda\}$.
If $\lambda \in \varLambda$ is maximal, then there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that $d_{\lambda \mu}=1$ and $d_{\lambda \nu}=0$ for all $\nu \in \varLambda^+ \setminus \{ \mu\}$.
nodes.label: C Lem min

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (minimal and maximal cell indices)
nodes.statement:
(\roman{ichi}) follows from Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}) immediately. 
We prove (\roman{ni}). 
Since we assume that $A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra, 
$A$ is a weakly symmetric algebra by Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}). 

Let $\lambda \in \varLambda$ be maximal and choose a linear extension which ends with $\lambda$. 
Assume that there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that $d_{\lambda \mu} \geq 2$. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ni}), 
we see that $P(\mu)$ contains $\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus d_{\lambda \mu}}$ as an $A$-submodule, 
which implies that $\operatorname{Soc} P(\mu)$ is not irreducible. It contradicts with 
$\operatorname{Top} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong L(\mu)$. 
Thus, we have $d_{\lambda \mu} \leq 1$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+$. 
Next, assume that there exist $\mu, \nu \in \varLambda^+$ ($\mu \not=\nu$) 
such that $d_{\lambda \mu}= d_{\lambda \nu}=1$. 
Then, by the same reasoning, both $P(\mu)$ and $P(\nu)$ contain $\Delta(\lambda)$ as an $A$-submodule. It follows that 
we have 
$L(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$ 
and 
$L(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$. 
However, $L(\mu)$ and $L(\nu)$ are inequivalent $A$-modules by Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (ii).
Thus, we have (\roman{ni}).
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Part (ii) by contradiction: a repeated or doubled cell module at the top of $P(\mu)$ would make its socle non-simple, contradicting weak symmetry.

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: (\roman{ichi}) follows from Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}) immediately.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Part (i) follows from unitriangularity of the decomposition matrix.

nodes.name: Weak symmetry
nodes.statement:
We prove (\roman{ni}). 
Since we assume that $A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra, 
$A$ is a weakly symmetric algebra by Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}).
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: For (ii), $A$ is weakly symmetric by the Koenig-Xi result.

nodes.name: Multiplicities at most one
nodes.statement:
Let $\lambda \in \varLambda$ be maximal and choose a linear extension which ends with $\lambda$. 
Assume that there exists $\mu \in \varLambda^+$ such that $d_{\lambda \mu} \geq 2$. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ni}), 
we see that $P(\mu)$ contains $\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus d_{\lambda \mu}}$ as an $A$-submodule, 
which implies that $\operatorname{Soc} P(\mu)$ is not irreducible. It contradicts with 
$\operatorname{Top} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong L(\mu)$. 
Thus, we have $d_{\lambda \mu} \leq 1$ for all $\mu \in \varLambda^+$.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: If $d_{\lambda\mu}\ge2$, $P(\mu)$ contains $\Delta(\lambda)^{\oplus2}$ and has non-simple socle.

nodes.name: Only one nonzero entry
nodes.statement:
Next, assume that there exist $\mu, \nu \in \varLambda^+$ ($\mu \not=\nu$) 
such that $d_{\lambda \mu}= d_{\lambda \nu}=1$. 
Then, by the same reasoning, both $P(\mu)$ and $P(\nu)$ contain $\Delta(\lambda)$ as an $A$-submodule. It follows that 
we have 
$L(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\mu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$ 
and 
$L(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} P(\nu) \cong \operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda)$. 
However, $L(\mu)$ and $L(\nu)$ are inequivalent $A$-modules by Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (ii).
Thus, we have (\roman{ni}).
nodes.section: Cellular algebras
nodes.statement_short: Two distinct $\mu,\nu$ would give $L(\mu)\cong L(\nu)$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Strategy 1: reduce to Skowronski's list
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ichi}) and our assumption that $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$, 
it is enough to classify basic self-injective cellular algebras of polynomial growth 
up to isomorphism of algebras.  
Since basic self-injective algebras over an algebraically closed field of polynomial growth 
have been classified by several authors, 
and they are listed in \cite{S}, 
it is enough to specify cellular algebras in the list of algebras from \cite{S}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Strategy 2: exhibit a cellular basis
nodes.statement:
In order to prove that a basic algebra listed in \cite{S} is cellular,
it is enough to give a cellular basis explicitly.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Strategy 3: contradiction on an idempotent truncation
nodes.statement:
In order to prove that a basic algebra listed in \cite{S} is not cellular, 
it is enough to give a contradiction to a property of cellular algebras given in this section 
for a cellular algebra with a small number of simple modules which is obtained from the original basic algebra 
by applying Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}.
nodes.section: Cellular algebras

nodes.name: Standing assumption on the base field
nodes.statement:
Throughout the paper, 
we always assume that $K$ is an algebraically closed field of $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$.

nodes.name: Standard self-injective algebra
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.8]{S} and $\operatorname{char} K \not=2$, the self-injective algebras we consider in this section are standard, 
that is, it admits a simply connected Galois covering whose Galois group is an admissible torsion-free group of $K$-linear automorphisms.

differentia: it admits a simply connected Galois covering whose Galois group is an admissible torsion-free group of $K$-linear automorphisms.

nodes.name: Classification of standard symmetric algebras of finite type
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.11]{S}, 
a nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebra of finite type is isomorphic to one of the following algebras: 
\begin{itemize}
\item 
A Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree has at most one exceptional vertex. 

\item 
A modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$ 
associated to a Brauer tree $T_S$ 
with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$. 

\item 
A trivial extension $T(B)$ of a tilted algebra $B$ of Dynkin type. 
\end{itemize}
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebras of finite type are Brauer tree, modified Brauer tree, or trivial extensions of tilted Dynkin algebras.
assumptions: a nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebra of finite type
conclusions: is isomorphic to one of the following algebras:

nodes.name: Cellular Brauer tree algebras (Koenig-Xi)
nodes.statement:
A Brauer tree algebra is cellular 
if and only if
the Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: A Brauer tree algebra is cellular if and only if the Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Prop BT

nodes.name: Remark on exceptional vertices in Koenig-Xi
nodes.statement:
In \cite[Proposition 5.3]{KX1}, 
Brauer trees are allowed to have an arbitrary number of exceptional vertices. 
However, in the above classification of nonsimple basic standard symmetric algebras of finite type, 
we consider only  Brauer trees with at most one exceptional vertex $S$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Argument that the modified Brauer tree is a line
nodes.statement:
By the definition of $D(T_S)$, 
if the Brauer tree $T_S$ has a branch, 
then the quiver of $D(T_S)$ contains a cycle whose length is at least $3$, 
and this cycle has no inverse arrow. 
This contradicts Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (\roman{san}) if $D(T_S)$ is cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A branch creates a cycle of length at least 3 without inverse arrows, contradicting the Ext-symmetry.

nodes.name: Cellular modified Brauer tree algebras have line-shaped trees
nodes.statement:
Thus, we see that 
the Brauer tree $T_S$ is a straight line if $D(T_S)$ is cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: the Brauer tree $T_S$ is a straight line

nodes.name: Ten-dimensional two-vertex algebra is not cellular
nodes.statement:
Let $A=KQ / I$ where
\[
\xymatrix{Q = & 1 \ar@(ul,dl)_{\gamma } \ar[r]<0.5 ex>^{\alpha_1}  & 2 \ar[l]<0.5 ex>^{\beta_1}}
\]
and $I$ is the two-sided ideal generated by 
$\{ \beta_1 \alpha_1, \, \gamma^2 - \alpha_1 \beta_1\}$. 
Then, $\dim A = 10$ and $A$ is not cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: The 10-dimensional algebra with a loop $\gamma$, $\beta_1\alpha_1=0$, $\gamma^2=\alpha_1\beta_1$ is not cellular.
assumptions: $I$ is the two-sided ideal generated by $\{ \beta_1 \alpha_1, \, \gamma^2 - \alpha_1 \beta_1\}$.
conclusions: $\dim A = 10$ and $A$ is not cellular.
nodes.label: F Lemma DB 2

nodes.name: Proof that the 10-dimensional algebra is not cellular
nodes.statement:
We see that 
\begin{align*}
& A e_1 = K e_1 \oplus K \gamma \oplus K \beta_1 \oplus K \gamma^2 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \oplus K \gamma^3, 
\\
& A e_2 = K e_2 \oplus K \alpha_1 \oplus K \gamma \alpha_1 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \alpha_1, 
\end{align*} 
and the Cartan matrix of $A$ is
\[
\mathbf C= \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
Suppose that $A$ is a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\varLambda, \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$. 
Let $\mathbf D$ be the decomposition matrix of the cellular structure of $A$. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), 
we have 
\[
\mathbf D^T \mathbf D = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
As Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}) tells us that every column of $D$ must contain $1$ as an entry, this equation implies that 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D= (d_{ij})_{1\leq i \leq 4, 1 \leq j \leq 2}=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1& 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\end{align*} 
modulo rearrangement of rows.  
Let $\varLambda=\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2, \lambda_3,\lambda_4\}$ and $\varLambda^+=\{ \mu_1, \mu_2\}$ be  such that 
$[ \Delta(\lambda_i) : L(\mu_j) ] = d_{ij}$. If $\lambda_1$ or $\lambda_2$ was maximal or minimal with respect to the partial order, then 
the corresponding row of $D$ would be a unit vector by Lemma \ref{C Lem min}, a contradiction. Thus, 
we can assume that 
a total order on $\varLambda$ which extends the partial order is 
$3<1<2<4$. In particular, we do not have $\lambda_1>\lambda_2$ in the partial order. 
We also note that $\mu = \min\{ \lambda \in \varLambda \mid d_{\lambda\mu}\ne0 \}$, for $\mu\in \varLambda^+$, by 
Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}). As $d_{\lambda_i\mu_2}\ne0$ only for $i=1,2$, $\mu_2\in\{\lambda_1,\lambda_2\}$, but
$\mu_2=\lambda_2$ contradicts $\lambda_1\not>\lambda_2$, so that $\mu_2=\lambda_1$. The minimality of $\lambda_3$ implies
$\mu_1=\lambda_3$ by Lemma \ref{C Lem min}(i).

We determine $A(\lambda_4)$ and $A(\lambda_2)$. By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ni}), 
we see that 
\begin{align}

A(\lambda_4) e_1 \cong P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_4), 
\quad 
A(\lambda_4) e_2 \cong P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_4} =0. 
\end{align}
As $A (\lambda_4)$ is a two-sided-ideal and $\Delta(\lambda_4) \cong L(\mu_1)$, 
\eqref{F DB 2} implies that $A(\lambda_4) = K \gamma^3$. 
In a similar way, we see that 
\begin{align}

\begin{split}
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 \cong P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_2} / P(\mu_1)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_2), 
\\
&(A(\lambda_2) / A(\lambda_4)) e_2 \cong P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_2} / P(\mu_2)_{\lambda_4} \cong \Delta(\lambda_2). 
\end{split}
\end{align}
Note that $A (\lambda_2)$ is a two-sided-ideal and $[ \Delta(\lambda_2) ] = [L(\mu_1)] + [L(\mu_2)]$.  
Then, since $\dim e_1(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 = 1$, there is a nonzero element $ae_1+b\gamma+c\gamma^2$ in $A(\lambda_2)e_1$. If $a\ne0$ 
then $a\gamma+b\gamma^2 \in A(\lambda_2)e_1$, which implies $\dim e_1(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1>1$. 
Thus, $a=0$. The same argument shows $b=0$ and we conclude that $\gamma^2\in A(\lambda_2)e_1$. On the other hand, $\dim e_2(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 = 1$
implies that there is a nonzero element $a\beta_1+b\beta_1\gamma$ in $A(\lambda_2)e_1$. 
We may also prove $\beta_1\gamma\alpha_1 \in A(\lambda_2)e_2$ and $\gamma\alpha_1 \in A(\lambda_2)e_2$ in the similar manner. Hence,
\begin{align*}
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4)) e_1 \equiv K \gamma^2 \oplus K (a\beta_1 + b\beta_1\gamma) \mod A (\lambda_4), 
\\ 
&(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2 \equiv K \gamma \alpha_1 \oplus K \beta_1 \gamma \alpha_1 \mod A (\lambda_4).
\end{align*}
We observe that $\alpha_1$ acts as zero on $(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2$. Then, $\alpha_1(a\beta_1 + b\beta_1\gamma) \equiv a\gamma^2$ implies $a=0$. 
However, if $a=0$ then we meet another contradiction
\begin{align*}
&\operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda_2) \cong \operatorname{Soc} (A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4)) e_1 \cong L(\mu_1) \oplus L(\mu_2), 
\\ 
&\operatorname{Soc} \Delta(\lambda_2) \cong  \operatorname{Soc} (A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4))e_2 \cong  L(\mu_2).
\end{align*}
We have proved that $A$ is not cellular.

On the other hand, $\dim e_2(A(\lambda_2)/ A(\lambda_4) )e_1 = 1$

nodes.name: Modified Brauer tree algebras are not cellular
nodes.statement:
A modified Brauer tree algebra $D(T_S)$ 
associated to any Brauer tree $T_S$ 
with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$ 
is not cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: associated to any Brauer tree $T_S$ with at least two edges and an extreme exceptional vertex $S$ of multiplicity $2$
conclusions: is not cellular.
nodes.label: F Prop MBD

nodes.name: Proof that modified Brauer tree algebras are not cellular
nodes.statement:
If $D (T_S)$ is a cellular algebra, 
the Brauer tree $T_S$ has to be a straight line by the argument in \ref{F BD}. 
On the other hand, 
if $T_S$ is a straight line with $n$ edges, 
then we have $D(T_S) = KQ_{T_S}/ I_{T_S}$, 
where $Q_{T_S}$ and $I_{T_S}$ are given by \eqref{F QTS} and \eqref{F ITS} respectively. 
Moreover, if we denote the algebra from Lemma \ref{F Lemma DB 2} by $A$,
we see that $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2) \cong A$. 
Indeed, if we compute bases of $D(T_S)e_1$ and $D(T_S)e_2$ explicitly, we know that 
$\dim (e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2) = 10$ 
and that we have a surjective algebra homomorphism $A \to (e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$. 
Thus, $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{F Lemma DB 2}, 
so that $D(T_S)$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}.

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a straight line, then the corner $(e_1+e_2)D(T_S)(e_1+e_2)$ is the non-cellular 10-dimensional algebra.

If $D (T_S)$ is a cellular algebra,

nodes.name: Cellular trivial extensions force radical square zero
nodes.statement:
Let $Q$ be a finite acyclic quiver, 
$I$ an admissible ideal of $K Q$. 
Put $A= KQ/I$. 
If the trivial extension $T(A)$ of $A$ is cellular, 
then we have $I= R^2_Q$, 
where $R_Q$ is the arrow ideal of $KQ$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: the trivial extension $T(A)$ of $A$ is cellular
conclusions: we have $I= R^2_Q$
nodes.label: F Lemma TA

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (trivial extensions)
nodes.statement:
We consider a bounded quiver presentation of $T(A)$. 
For this, we need add new arrows to $Q$ which generate $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,K)$. 
Then, we obtain 
the quiver $Q_{T(A)}$ of $T(A)$ from the quiver of $Q$ by the following 
recipe\footnote{Since $T(A)$ is the quotient of the repetitive algebra 
by the Nakayama automorphism $\nu_A$, 
we may also obtain the presentation by 
using the bounded quiver presentation of the repetitive algebra of $A$ 
given in \cite[Lemma 1.3]{A}.}: 
\begin{quote}
\it
Let $\alpha$ be a path in $Q$ such that $\alpha \not \in I$ and $\beta \alpha, \alpha \beta \in I$ for any arrow $\beta$ in $Q$.
Then we add an arrow from $t(\alpha)$ to $s(\alpha)$, 
where $t(\alpha)$ is the target of $\alpha$ and $s(\alpha)$ is the source of $\alpha$.  
\end{quote}
Thanks to this construction, 
if there exists a path $\alpha$ in $Q$ such that the length of $\alpha$ is at least $2$ and $\alpha \not\in I$, 
then $Q_{T(A)}$ contains a cycle whose length is at least $3$, 
and this cycle has no inverse arrow. 
This contradicts Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (\roman{san}) if $T(A)$ is cellular. 
We have proved $R_Q^2\subset I$. 
The opposite inclusion is clear since $I$ is an admissible ideal.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero path of length $\ge2$ creates a new arrow closing a cycle of length $\ge3$ without inverse arrows, contradicting Ext-symmetry.

nodes.name: Quiver of $T(A)$
nodes.statement:
We consider a bounded quiver presentation of $T(A)$. 
For this, we need add new arrows to $Q$ which generate $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,K)$. 
Then, we obtain 
the quiver $Q_{T(A)}$ of $T(A)$ from the quiver of $Q$ by the following 
recipe\footnote{Since $T(A)$ is the quotient of the repetitive algebra 
by the Nakayama automorphism $\nu_A$, 
we may also obtain the presentation by 
using the bounded quiver presentation of the repetitive algebra of $A$ 
given in \cite[Lemma 1.3]{A}.}: 
\begin{quote}
\it
Let $\alpha$ be a path in $Q$ such that $\alpha \not \in I$ and $\beta \alpha, \alpha \beta \in I$ for any arrow $\beta$ in $Q$.
Then we add an arrow from $t(\alpha)$ to $s(\alpha)$, 
where $t(\alpha)$ is the target of $\alpha$ and $s(\alpha)$ is the source of $\alpha$.  
\end{quote}
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Describe new arrows of $T(A)$ for maximal nonzero paths.

nodes.name: Radical square zero
nodes.statement:
Thanks to this construction, 
if there exists a path $\alpha$ in $Q$ such that the length of $\alpha$ is at least $2$ and $\alpha \not\in I$, 
then $Q_{T(A)}$ contains a cycle whose length is at least $3$, 
and this cycle has no inverse arrow. 
This contradicts Proposition \ref{C Prop simple} (\roman{san}) if $T(A)$ is cellular. 
We have proved $R_Q^2\subset I$. 
The opposite inclusion is clear since $I$ is an admissible ideal.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A long nonzero path gives a cycle without inverse arrows, so $R_Q^2\subset I$.

nodes.name: Double quiver $\widehat{Q}$
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Lemma 1.3]{A} (see the proof of Lemma \ref{F Lemma TA}), 
we see that the quiver of $T(KQ/R_Q^2)$ is the double quiver 
$\widehat{Q}=(\widehat{Q}_0, \widehat{Q}_1)$ of $Q$, 
namely $\widehat{Q}_0=Q_0$ and $\widehat{Q}_1$ is obtained from $Q_1$ by adding an additional arrow $\alpha^*$ 
for each $\alpha \in Q_1$ such that $s(\alpha^*) = t(\alpha)$ and $t(\alpha^*)=s (\alpha)$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: The quiver of $T(KQ/R_Q^2)$ is the double quiver obtained by adding a reversed arrow $\alpha^*$ for each arrow $\alpha$.

nodes.name: Ideal $I_{\widehat{Q}}$
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Zero relations on non-returning paths and commutativity relations $\alpha\alpha^*=\beta^*\beta$ etc.

nodes.name: Trivial extension of a radical-square-zero algebra
nodes.statement:
Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite acyclic quiver, 
and $R_Q$ be the arrow ideal of $KQ$. 
Then the trivial extension $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$ 
is isomorphic to $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: the trivial extension $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$ is isomorphic to $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$.
nodes.label: F Lemma KQ RQ2

nodes.name: Proof of the trivial extension presentation
nodes.statement:
Let $\{f_{i} \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{ f_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in Q_1\} \subset \operatorname{Hom}_{K} (KQ/ R_Q^2, K)$ 
be the dual basis of the basis
$\{e_i \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{\alpha \in Q_1\}$ of $KQ/ R_Q^2$,
namely $f_{i}(e_j)=\delta_{ij}$, $f_{i}(\alpha)=0$, $f_{\alpha}(e_i)=0$ and $f_{\alpha}(\beta) = \delta_{\alpha \beta}$, 
for $i,j \in Q_0$ and $\alpha, \beta \in Q_1$. 
Then
\begin{align*}
\{e_i \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{\alpha \in Q_1\} \cup \{f_{i} \mid i \in Q_0\} \cup \{ f_{\alpha} \mid \alpha \in Q_1\}
\end{align*}
gives a basis of $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$. 
Checking the well-definedness by direct calculation,
we can define an algebra homomorphism $\Phi: K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} \rightarrow T (KQ/ R_Q^2)$ by
\begin{align*} 
e_i \mapsto e_i \, (i \in Q_0), \, 
\alpha \mapsto \alpha, \, \alpha^* \mapsto f_{\alpha} \, (\alpha \in Q_1). 
\end{align*} 
In particular, we used
$\alpha f_{\alpha} = f_{s(\alpha)}$ and $f_\alpha \alpha = f_{t (\alpha)}$ in $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$, for $\alpha \in Q_1$, 
in the calculation, and they also show that
$\Phi$ is surjective. 
By comparing the dimensions of $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ and $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$, 
we see that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Map $\alpha^*$ to dual basis elements $f_\alpha$; the map is a surjective homomorphism and dimensions agree.

nodes.name: Basis of the trivial extension
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Dual basis gives a basis of $T(KQ/R_Q^2)$.

nodes.name: Homomorphism $\Phi$
nodes.statement:

\end{align*} 
In particular, we used

nodes.name: Isomorphism
nodes.statement:
By comparing the dimensions of $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ and $T(KQ/ R_Q^2)$, 
we see that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Dimensions agree, so $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Underlying graph $\overline{Q}$
nodes.statement: We denote the underlying graph of $Q$ by $\overline{Q}$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Cellularity of $K\widehat{Q}/I_{\widehat{Q}}$
nodes.statement:
Let $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite connected acyclic quiver. 
Then, 
the algebra 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular 
if and only if 
the underlying graph $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$ is a straight line with no multiple edge.
Furthermore, if the condition holds then
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose
Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: $Q=(Q_0,Q_1)$ be a finite connected acyclic quiver.
conclusions: the algebra $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular if and only if the underlying graph $\overline{Q}$ of $Q$ is a straight line with no multiple edge.
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Prop hatQ hatI

nodes.name: Proof of the cellularity criterion for $K\widehat{Q}/I_{\widehat{Q}}$
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular.
If $\overline{Q}$ has a multiple edge, 
then $Q$ contains a subquiver 
\[
\xymatrix{Q' =  i \ar[rr]<-1.5ex>   \ar[rr]<1.8ex> & \vdots  & j }
\]
with $k$ arrows ($k \geq 2$) by Proposition \ref{C Prop simple}.  
By the defining relations, 
we see that $(e_i + e_j)(K\widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}})(e_i + e_j) \cong K \widehat{Q'} / I_{\widehat{Q'}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is
\[
\mathbf C'=\begin{pmatrix} 2 & k \\ k & 2 \end{pmatrix}. 
\]
By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{yon}), 
$(e_i + e_j)(K\widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}})(e_i + e_j)$ is not cellular 
since $\det \mathbf C' \leq 0$. 
Then, by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}, 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular, contradicting our assumption. Hence
$\overline{Q}$ has no multiple edge. 

Note that $Q$ does not have an oriented cycle since $Q$ is acyclic. In particular 
the underlying graph of $Q$ does not contain a loop.
Suppose that $Q$ contains a subquiver $Q^{\sharp}$ 
whose underlying graph is a cycle of length $l\ge2$. We label its vertices as follows. 
\begin{align*}
\xymatrix@R=3pt{
&i_2 \ar@{-}[r] & i_3 \ar@{-}[dr]  &
\\
&&& \ar@{.}[dd]
\\
\overline{Q^{\sharp}} = i_1\ar@{-}[uur] &&& & 
\\
&&& \ar@{-}[dl]
\\
& i_l \ar@{-}[uul]& i_{l-1} \ar@{-}[l] &
}
\end{align*}
Then we see that 
$(e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) (K\widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}) (e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) 
	\cong K \widehat{Q^{\sharp}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\sharp}}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf C^{\sharp} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 
	\\ 
	1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	&&&&& \vdots &&&&
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1
	\\
	1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2
	\end{pmatrix}. 
\end{align*}
Suppose that $K \widehat{Q^{\sharp}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\sharp}}}$ is a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\varLambda,\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C}, \iota)$,  
and let $\mathbf D^{\sharp}$ be its decomposition matrix. 
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), 
we have 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf D^{\sharp} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 1 
	\\
	1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	&&&& \vdots &&&
        \\
        0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & 1 & 0
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 1 
	\end{pmatrix}. 
\end{align*}
modulo rearrangement of rows.

Put $\varLambda =\{ \lambda_1, \lambda_2,\dots, \lambda_{l}\}$
such that $([\Delta(\lambda_i) : L(\lambda_j)])_{1\leq i,j \leq l} = \mathbf D^{\sharp}$.  
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}), 
we have 
$\lambda_l < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \dots < \lambda_{l-1} < \lambda_l$ in the partial order, which is impossible. Hence, 
$(e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l}) (K\widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}) (e_{i_1} + \dots + e_{i_l})$ 
is not cellular, and 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}, contradicting our assumption again.   

Assume that $\overline{Q}$ has no multiple edge and no cycle. 
If $\overline{Q}$ has a branch, 
$Q$ contains a subquiver $Q^{\natural}$ whose underlying graph is of the following form
\begin{align*}
&\xymatrix@R=5pt{ & & i_3 \\ \overline{Q^{\natural}} = i_1 \ar@{-}[r] & i_2 \ar@{-}[ur] \ar@{-}[dr] & & \\ && i_4}
\end{align*}
We see that 
$(e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} (e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) 
	\cong K \widehat{Q^{\natural}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\natural}}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf C^{\natural} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	2 & 1 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	1 & 2 & 1 & 1 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 2 & 0 
	\\
	0 & 1 & 0 & 2
	\end{pmatrix}.
\end{align*} 
However, 
there is no matrix $\mathbf D$ with non-negative integral entries that satisfies 
$\mathbf D^T \mathbf D = \mathbf C$. 
Thus, 
$(e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} (e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4})$ 
is not cellular by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{san}), and 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is not cellular by Lemma \ref{C Lem idem}. 

Now the only graph $\overline{Q}$ without cycles or loops, 
and branch points, is a straight line. Hence we have proved that 
$\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge if $K \widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular. 

Conversely, suppose that $\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge. Then we easily see that 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra 
whose Brauer tree is a straight line  
with no exceptional vertex, which is cellular by Proposition \ref{F Prop BT}.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Exclude multiple edges, cycles and branch points by idempotent truncations whose Cartan matrices admit no decomposition matrix; the line case is a Brauer tree algebra.

nodes.name: No multiple edges
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular.
If $\overline{Q}$ has a multiple edge, 
then $Q$ contains a subquiver 
\[

nodes.statement_short: A multiple edge gives a corner with Cartan determinant $\le0$.

nodes.statement:

	\\
	&&&&& \vdots &&&&
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1
	\\
	1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2

\end{align*}

\mathbf D^{\sharp} =

	\\

	\\

        \\
        0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & 1 & 0
	\\
	0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 1 & 1 
	\end{pmatrix}. 
\end{align*}
modulo rearrangement of rows.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A cycle in $\overline{Q}$ gives a corner with cyclic Cartan matrix.

nodes.name: Cycle impossible
nodes.statement:
Put $\varLambda =\{ \lambda_1, \lambda_2,\dots, \lambda_{l}\}$
such that $([\Delta(\lambda_i) : L(\lambda_j)])_{1\leq i,j \leq l} = \mathbf D^{\sharp}$.  
Then, by Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} (\roman{ichi}),

nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: The forced decomposition matrix yields a cyclic order, impossible.

nodes.name: No branch
nodes.statement:
Assume that $\overline{Q}$ has no multiple edge and no cycle. 
If $\overline{Q}$ has a branch, 
$Q$ contains a subquiver $Q^{\natural}$ whose underlying graph is of the following form
\begin{align*}
&\xymatrix@R=5pt{ & & i_3 \\ \overline{Q^{\natural}} = i_1 \ar@{-}[r] & i_2 \ar@{-}[ur] \ar@{-}[dr] & & \\ && i_4}
\end{align*}
We see that 
$(e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}} (e_{i_1}+ \dots + e_{i_4}) 
	\cong K \widehat{Q^{\natural}}/ I_{\widehat{Q^{\natural}}}$, 
and its Cartan matrix is 
\begin{align*}
\mathbf C^{\natural} = 
	\begin{pmatrix} 
	2 & 1 & 0 & 0 
	\\
	1 & 2 & 1 & 1 
	\\

	\\

	\end{pmatrix}.

nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A branch point gives a Cartan matrix with no factorisation.

nodes.name: Straight line
nodes.statement:
Now the only graph $\overline{Q}$ without cycles or loops, 
and branch points, is a straight line. Hence we have proved that 
$\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge if $K \widehat{Q} / I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is cellular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement:
Conversely, suppose that $\overline{Q}$ is a straight line with no multiple edge. Then we easily see that 
$K \widehat{Q}/ I_{\widehat{Q}}$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra 
whose Brauer tree is a straight line  
with no exceptional vertex, which is cellular by Proposition \ref{F Prop BT}.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A line gives a Brauer tree algebra, cellular by Koenig-Xi.

nodes.name: Proof of the trivial extension criterion
nodes.statement:
Note that 
the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex is
isomorphic to the trivial extension of a tilted algebra of type $A_n$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$.
Hence, we obtain the following proposition as a special case of Proposition \ref{F Prop hatQ hatI}.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Special case of the criterion for $K\widehat{Q}/I_{\widehat{Q}}$, since line Brauer tree algebras are trivial extensions of tilted algebras of type $A_n$.

nodes.name: Cellular trivial extensions of tilted Dynkin algebras
nodes.statement:
The trivial extension $T(B)$ of a tilted algebra $B$ of Dynkin type 
is cellular 
if and only if 
$T(B)$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is 
a straight line with no exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: The trivial extension $T(B)$ of a tilted algebra $B$ of Dynkin type
conclusions: is cellular if and only if $T(B)$ is isomorphic to the Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with no exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Prop TE

nodes.name: Proof of the symmetric finite type classification
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 3.11]{S}, Proposition \ref{F Prop BT}, Proposition \ref{F Prop MBD} and Proposition \ref{F Prop TE}, 
we have the following proposition.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Combine Skowronski's list with the three cellularity criteria.

nodes.name: Basic symmetric cellular algebras of finite type (Ohmatsu)
nodes.statement:
An algebra $A$ is a basic symmetric cellular algebra of finite type 
if and only if 
$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra
whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
conclusions: An algebra $A$ is a basic symmetric cellular algebra of finite type if and only if $A$ is isomorphic to a Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Prop symmetric

nodes.name: Weakly symmetric algebras of finite type are symmetric
nodes.statement: A weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type is symmetric.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: A weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type
conclusions: is symmetric.
nodes.label: F Prop weak

nodes.name: Proof via the Stamm-algebra
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a basic weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type, 
and $A'$ be its Stamm-algebra (see \cite[Definition 4.4]{W} for the definition of Stamm-algebra). 
By \cite[Coroollary 4.7 (\roman{san}) in Part I]{W}, $A'$ is symmetric if and only if $A$ is weakly symmetric. 
If $A$ was not a symmetric algebra, then 
$A$ would be isomorphic to $A'$ by \cite[Theorem C]{KS}, 
which contradicts with $A'$ being a symmetric algebra.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction using Waschbuesch's Stamm-algebra and the Kupisch-Scherzler theorem.

nodes.name: Stamm-algebra
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a basic weakly symmetric algebra over $K$ of finite type, 
and $A'$ be its Stamm-algebra (see \cite[Definition 4.4]{W} for the definition of Stamm-algebra). 
By \cite[Coroollary 4.7 (\roman{san}) in Part I]{W}, $A'$ is symmetric if and only if $A$ is weakly symmetric.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: The Stamm-algebra $A'$ is symmetric iff $A$ is weakly symmetric.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement:
If $A$ was not a symmetric algebra, then 
$A$ would be isomorphic to $A'$ by \cite[Theorem C]{KS}, 
which contradicts with $A'$ being a symmetric algebra.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: A non-symmetric $A$ would equal its symmetric Stamm-algebra.

nodes.name: Proof of the finite type theorem
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv} (\roman{ni}), 
Proposition \ref{F Prop symmetric}
and 
Proposition \ref{F Prop weak}, 
we have the following theorem.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement_short: Self-injective cellular implies weakly symmetric, hence symmetric in finite type; then apply the symmetric classification.

nodes.name: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a basic algebra over $K$. 
The following are equivalent. 
\begin{enumerate} 
\item 
$A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra of finite type. 

\item 
$A$ is isomorphic  to a Brauer tree algebra 
whose Brauer tree is
a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex. 
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of finite type
assumptions: Let $A$ be a basic algebra over $K$.
conclusions: $A$ is a self-injective cellular algebra of finite type.
$A$ is isomorphic to a Brauer tree algebra whose Brauer tree is a straight line with at most one exceptional vertex.
nodes.label: F Theorem

nodes.name: Reduction to weakly symmetric algebras with nonsingular Cartan matrix
nodes.statement:
By Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix} and Proposition \ref{C Prop Morita equiv},  
it suffices to consider weakly symmetric algebras of domestic type whose Cartan matrices are nonsingular.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type

nodes.name: Standard domestic self-injective algebras are of Euclidean type
nodes.statement:
By \cite[Theorem 4.3]{S}, a self-injective algebra is standard domestic of infinite type 
if and only if it is a self-injective algebra of Euclidean type.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
conclusions: a self-injective algebra is standard domestic of infinite type if and only if it is a self-injective algebra of Euclidean type.

nodes.name: Common assumption on the Brauer graphs
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
nodes.statement_short: The Brauer graphs have at most one cycle, of odd length if it exists.

nodes.name: Brauer quiver $Q_T$
nodes.statement: Given a Brauer graph $T$, we denote by $Q_{T}$ the Brauer quiver associated with $T$.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type

nodes.name: $\alpha$-parts, $\beta$-parts, $\gamma$-cycle and $\delta$-cycle
nodes.statement:
The cyclic ordering of each vertex in $T$ defines two simple cycles in $Q_{T}$ if it is the endpoint of a loop, and
one simple cycle in $Q_{T}$ otherwise. In particular, 
if a distinguished vertex of $T$ is chosen, then it defines one or two distinguished simple cycles, say $\gamma$-cycle or $\delta$-cycle, in $Q_{T}$, 
and we divide the remaining simple cycles of $Q_{T}$ into $\alpha$-parts and $\beta$-parts 
in such a way that if two cycles intersect at a vertex in $Q_{T}$, then the two cycles belong to different parts.
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
nodes.statement_short: Simple cycles of $Q_T$ around a distinguished vertex are the $\gamma$/$\delta$-cycles; the rest split into $\alpha$- and $\beta$-parts so intersecting cycles lie in different parts.

nodes.name: $\alpha$-cycles and $\beta$-cycles
nodes.statement:
The cycles in the $\alpha$-parts (respectively, the $\beta$-parts) 
are called $\alpha$-cycles (respectively, $\beta$-cycles).

nodes.name: Arrow notation $\alpha_i$, $\alpha(i)$
nodes.statement:
We denote an arrow in the $\alpha$-parts (respectively, the $\beta$-parts, the $\gamma$-cycle, the $\delta$-cycle) 
which starts at a vertex $i$ by $\alpha _{i}$ (respectively, $\beta_{i}$, $\gamma_{i}$, $\delta_{i}$), 
and we denote the target of $\alpha_{i}$ (respectively, $\beta_{i}$, $\gamma_{i}$, $\delta_{i}$) by $\alpha(i)$ (respectively, $\beta(i)$, $\gamma(i)$, $\delta(i)$).

nodes.name: Cycle notation $A_i,B_i,C_i,D_i$
nodes.statement:
We will use the symbol $A_{i}$ (respectively, $B_{i}$, $C_{i}$, $D_{i}$) to denote the $\alpha$-cycle (respectively, $\beta$-cycle, $\gamma$-cycle, $\delta$-cycle) from $i$ to $i$, that is,
\[ \begin{array}{cc}
A_{i}=\alpha_{i}\alpha_{\alpha(i)}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(i)}, &  B_{i}=\beta_{i}\beta_{\beta(i)}\cdots\beta_{\beta^{-1}(i)} ,\\
C_{i}=\gamma_{i}\gamma_{\gamma(i)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(i)}, &  D_{i}=\delta_{i}\delta_{\delta(i)}\cdots\delta_{\delta^{-1}(i)}.
\end{array}\]

nodes.name: Algebra $\Lambda'(T)$
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be a Brauer graph with exactly one cycle, which is of an odd length, and we define $\Lambda'(T)$. 

Suppose that the cycle is not a loop, and that a distinguished vertex $v$ on the cycle is chosen. 
We call the simple cycle in $Q_T$ associated with the cyclic ordering around $v$ the $\gamma$-cycle. 
Then, $\Lambda'(T) = KQ_T/I'(T)$, where $I'(T)$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_i\beta_{\alpha(i)},$ $\beta_i\alpha_{\beta(i)},$ $\alpha_i\gamma_{\alpha(i)},$ $\gamma_i\alpha_{\gamma(i)},$  
$\gamma_i\beta_{\gamma(i)},$ $\beta_i\gamma_{\beta(i)}$, where $i$ are vertices of $Q_T$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle,
\item $A_j-C_j$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle,
\item $B_j-C_j$, where $j$ is the intersection of a $\beta$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle.
\end{enumerate} 

Suppose that the cycle is a loop, and the vertex of the loop is chosen as the distinguished vertex $v$. 
Then we have distinguished simple cycles the $\gamma$-cycle and the $\delta$-cycle in $Q_{T}$ 
which are associated with the cyclic ordering around $v$. 
We denote the intersection of the $\gamma$-cycle and the $\delta$-cycle by $a$.
Then, $\Lambda'(T) = KQ_T/I'(T)$, where $I'(T)$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_i\beta_{\alpha(i)},$ $\beta_i\alpha_{\beta(i)},$ $\alpha_i\gamma_{\alpha(i)},$ $\gamma_i\alpha_{\gamma(i)},$ 
$\gamma_i\beta_{\gamma(i)},$ $\beta_i\gamma_{\beta(i)},$ $\alpha_i\delta_{\alpha(i)},$ $\delta_i\alpha_{\delta(i)},$  
$\beta_i\delta_{\beta(i)},$ $\delta_i\beta_{\delta(i)}$, where $i$ are vertices of $Q_T$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle,
\item $A_j-\gamma_j\gamma_{\gamma(j)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(a)}D_{a}\gamma_{a}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(j)}$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle,
\item $A_j-\delta_j\delta_{\delta(j)}\cdots\delta_{\delta^{-1}(a)}C_{a}\delta_{a}\cdots\delta_{\delta^{-1}(j)}$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and the $\delta$-cycle,
\item $B_j-\gamma_j\gamma_{\gamma(j)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(a)}D_{a}\gamma_{a}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(j)}$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\beta$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle,
\item $B_j-\delta_j\delta_{\delta(j)}\cdots\delta_{\delta^{-1}(a)}C_{a}\delta_{a}\cdots\delta_{\delta^{-1}(j)}$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\beta$-cycle and the $\delta$-cycle,
\item $\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(a)}\gamma_{a}$, $\delta_{\delta^{-1}(a)}\delta_{a}$,
\item $C_{a}D_{a} - D_{a}C_{a}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Algebra $\Gamma^{(0)}(T,v)$
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be a Brauer graph with exactly one loop. 
We denote the loop and its vertex by $b$ and $u$ respectively. 
We assume that there is an edge $a$ of $T$ which is different from $b$ such that
\begin{itemize}
\item
the endpoints of $a$ are $u$ and $v$,
\item
no other edge than $a$ has $v$ as an endpoint,
\item
the edges $a$ and $b$ are direct successors of the other in the cyclic ordering around the vertex $u$,
\item
the loop $b$ is not a direct successor of itself in the cyclic ordering around the vertex $u$.
\end{itemize}
Then, we choose $u$ as the distinguished vertex and we define $\Gamma^{(0)}(T,v)$. 

Let two simple cycles in $Q_T$ associated with the cyclic ordering around $u$ be 
the $\gamma$-cycle and the $\delta$-cycle. They intersect at the vertex $b$ of $Q_T$. 
By the second condition, there is the unique loop in $Q_T$ which has the vertex $a$ as the endpoint. 
We assume that this loop belongs to $\alpha$-parts. We also assume that 
the simple cycle $b\to a \to b$ is the $\delta$-cycle, so that $D_b=\delta_b\delta_a$. Then,
$\Gamma^{(0)}(T,v) = KQ_T/I^{(0)}(T,v)$, where $I^{(0) }(T,v)$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_i\beta_{\alpha(i)},$ $\beta_i\alpha_{\beta(i)},$ $\alpha_i\gamma_{\alpha(i)},$ $\gamma_i\alpha_{\gamma(i)},$  
$\gamma_i\beta_{\gamma(i)},$ $\beta_i\gamma_{\beta(i)}$, where $i$ are vertices of $Q_T$, and 
$\alpha_a\delta_a,$ $\delta_b\alpha_a$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle,
\item $A_j-\gamma_j\gamma_{\gamma(j)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(b)}D_b\gamma_b\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(j)}$, 
where $j$ is the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle,
\item $\alpha_{a} - \delta_{a}C_{b}\delta_{b}$,
\item $B_j-\gamma_j\gamma_{\gamma(j)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(b)}D_b\gamma_b\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(j)}$, 
where $j$ is the intersection of an $\beta$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle,
\item $\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(b)}\gamma_{b}$,
\item $\delta_{a}C_{b}-\delta_{a}D_{b}$,
\item $C_{b}\delta_{b}-D_{b}\delta_{b}$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: $KQ_T/I^{(0)}(T,v)$ for a Brauer graph with exactly one loop at $u$ and a pendant edge $a=uv$ adjacent to it.
nodes.label: D defn II

nodes.name: Algebra $\Gamma^{(1)}(T,v)$
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be a Brauer graph with a unique exceptional vertex $v$, whose multiplicity is two, 
and a unique cycle, which is of length three. When we draw the Brauer graph in a plane, 
we assume that
\begin{itemize}
\item
the label of the edges of the cycle is given as
 \[\begin{xy}
(0,0)*[o]+{v_{3}}="2",(30,0)*[o]+{v_{2}}="3",(15,10)*[o]+{v_{1}}="1",
\ar @{-}"1";"2"_{a}
\ar @{-}"2";"3"^{c}
\ar @{-}"1";"3"^{b}
\end{xy}\] 
and other edges are located outside the triangle, that is, 
$a$ (respectively, $b$, $c$) is the direct successor of $b$ (respectively, $c$, $a$) 
in the cyclic ordering around $v_{1}$ (respectively, $v_{2}$, $v_{3}$),
\item
among the vertices $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ and $v_{3}$, $v_{3}$ is the nearest vertex
to the exceptional vertex $v$, where $v=v_{3}$ may occur. 
\end{itemize}
Then, we choose $v_1$ as the distinguished vertex and we define $\Gamma^{(1)}(T,v)$.

Note that there is no cycle outside the triangle by the common assumption which we made for the Brauer graphs. 
We call the simple cycle in $Q_{T}$ associated with the cyclic ordering around $v_{1}$ the $\gamma$-cycle, 
and assume that the simple cycle associated with $v_{2}$ (respectively, $v_{3}$) belongs to $\beta$-parts (respectively, $\alpha$-parts). 
We call the simple cycle associated with the cyclic ordering around $v$ \emph{the exceptional cycle}. 
Then, $\Gamma^{(1)}(T,v) = KQ_T/I^{(1)}(T,v)$, where $I^{(1)}(T,v)$ is the ideal 
generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\beta_i\alpha_{\beta(i)},$ $\alpha_i\gamma_{\alpha(i)},$ $\gamma_i\beta_{\gamma(i)}$, where $i$ are vertices of $Q_T$,
\item $\alpha_{i}\beta_{\alpha(i)}$, for $i\ne a$,
\item $\gamma_{i}\alpha_{\gamma(i)}$, for $i\ne b$,
\item $\beta_{i}\gamma_{\beta(i)}$, for $i\ne c$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j\neq c$ and the two cycles are not exceptional,
\item $A_j-C_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle is a vertex $j\neq a$ and the two cycles are not exceptional,
\item $B_j-C_j$, if the intersection of a $\beta$-cycle and the $\gamma$-cycle is a vertex $j\neq b$ and the two cycles are not exceptional, 
\item $A_j^{2}-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j\neq c$ and the $\alpha$-cycle is exceptional,
\item $A_j-B_j^{2}$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and the $\beta$-cycle is exceptional,
\item $\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(b)}\gamma_{b}\alpha_{a},$ $\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(a)}\alpha_{a}\beta_{c}, \beta_{\beta^{-1}(c)}\beta_{c}\gamma_{b}$,
\item $\beta_{b}\beta_{\beta(b)}\cdots\beta_{\beta^{-1}(c)}-\gamma_{b}\alpha_{a},$ $\gamma_{a}\gamma_{\gamma(a)}\cdots\gamma_{\gamma^{-1}(b)}-\alpha_{a}\beta_{c}$,
\item $\alpha_{c}\alpha_{\alpha(c)}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(a)}-\beta_{c}\gamma_{b}$, if the $\alpha$-cycle through the vertex $c$ is not exceptional,
\item $\alpha_{c}\alpha_{\alpha(c)}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(a)}A_{a}-\beta_{c}\gamma_{b}$, if the $\alpha$-cycle through the vertex $c$ is exceptional.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.label: D defn III

nodes.name: Remark on the relations of $\Gamma^{(1)}(T,v)$
nodes.statement:
In fact, we have $j\ne a, b, c$ in the conditions (v)-(ix): if $j=a$ or $b$ in (v) then one of the cycles is the $\gamma$-cycle, that is, 
it is not an $\alpha$-cycle nor a $\beta$-cycle. The same reasoning excludes $j=b, c$ in (vi), $j=a, c$ in (vii) and $j=a, b$ in (viii). 
We have $j\ne c$ in (ix) because if $j=c$ then the $\beta$-cycle is not exceptional. 
Another remark is that the condition for 
$\alpha_i\beta_{\alpha(i)}$ (respectively, $\gamma_i\alpha_{\gamma(i)}$, $\beta_i\gamma_{\beta(i)}$) appears in (ii) and (xi) 
(respectively, (iii) and (xi), (iv) and (xii), (xiii)).

nodes.name: Algebra $\Lambda(T,v_1,v_2)$
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be a Brauer tree  $T$ (in the sense of \cite[Proposition 5.3]{KX1}) with two different exceptional vertices $v_{1}$ and  $v_{2}$ of multiplicity two. 
Then, we do not specify the distingushed vertex, so that there are no $\gamma$-cycle and $\delta$-cycle, 
and we define $\Lambda(T,v_{1},v_{2})$.

We call simple cycles associated with the cyclic ordering around the exceptional vertices $v_{1}$ and $v_{2}$ 
\emph{exceptional cycles}. Then, $\Lambda(T,v_{1},v_{2}) = KQ_T/I(T,v_{1},v_{2})$, 
where $I(T,v_{1},v_{2})$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_{i}\beta_{\alpha(i)},$ $\beta_{i}\alpha_{\beta(i)}$, where $i$ are vertices of $Q_{T}$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and 
the two cycles are not exceptional,
\item $A_j^{2}-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and 
only the $\alpha$-cycle is exceptional, 
\item $A_j-B_j^{2}$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and 
only the $\beta$-cycle is exceptional,
\item $A_j^{2}-B_j^{2}$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and 
both the $\alpha$-cycle and the $\beta$-cycle are exceptional.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.statement_short: Brauer tree algebra with two exceptional vertices of multiplicity two.
nodes.label: D defn IV

nodes.name: Algebra $\Gamma^{(2)}(T,v_1,v_2)$
nodes.statement:
Let $T$ be a Brauer tree with 
a unique exceptional vertex $v_{2}$
\footnote{In page 51 of \cite{BHS}, the definition starts with stating that $v_1$ and $v_2$ are exceptional vertices. 
However, it is stated in the middle of the page that the exceptional cycle is the one which is associated with the cyclic ordering around $v_2$. 
Thus, only $v_2$ is exceptional, and we should follow the definition in \cite{BS}.}
, which is of multiplicity two. 
We assume the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item
There is an edge $a$ of $T$ which has endpoints $v_1$ and $u$.
\item
The vertex $v_1$ is different from $v_2$ and $v_1$ is not an endpoint of any other edge than $a$.
\item
Let $b$ be the direct successor of $a$ and $c$ the direct predecessor of $a$ in the cyclic ordering around $u$. 
Then, $b\ne a$ and $c\ne a$.
\item
The vertices $u$, $v_{1}$, $v_{2}$ and the edges $a$, $b$, $c$ determine a subtree 
\[ 
 \begin{xy}
(0,0)*[o]+{v_{3}}="3",(20,0)*[o]+{u}="u",(10,-15)*[o]+{v_{1}}="1",(30,-15)*[o]+{\circ}="000",(40,0)*[o]+{\circ}="001",(50,0)*[o]+{}="dammy1",
(55,0)*[o]+{\cdots}="cdots",(60,0)*[o]+{}="dammy2",(70,0)*[o]+{\circ}="002",(90,0)*[o]+{v_{2}}="2"
\ar @{-}"3";"u"^{b}
\ar @{-}"1";"u"^{a}
\ar @{-}"000";"u"_{c}
\ar @{-}"u";"001"^{e}
\ar @{-}"001";"dammy1"
\ar @{-}"dammy2";"002"
\ar @{-}"002";"2"
\end{xy}
\]
of the Brauer tree $T$, where one of $u=v_{2}$, $v_{3}=v_{2}$ may occur (but cannot be both as $u\ne v_3$), 
and any of $b=e$, $c=e$ and $b=c=e$ may hold. 
\end{itemize}
Then, we do not specify the distinguished vertex and we define $\Gamma^{(2)}(T,v_{1},v_{2})$.

We call the simple cycle of $Q_T$ associated with the cyclic ordering around the vertex $v_2$ \emph{the exceptional cycle}. 
We assume that the simple cycle in $Q_{T}$ associated with the cyclic ordering around the vertex $u$ is an $\alpha$-cycle. 
Then, $\Gamma^{(2)}(T,v_{1},v_{2}) = KQ_T^{(2)}/I^{(2)}(T,v_{1},v_{2})$, where the vertices and the arrows of $Q_{T}^{(2)}$ are given by
\[ Q_{T}^{(2)}=((Q_{T})_{0}\cup \{ w\},\ (Q_{T})_{1}\cup\{ \gamma_{1}:c\to w,\ \gamma_{2}: w\to b,\ \gamma_{3}:w\to w\}),\]
and $I^{(2)}(T,v_{1},v_{2})$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_{i}\beta_{\alpha(i)}$, $\beta_{i}\alpha_{\beta(i)}$, for all vertices $i$ of $Q_{T}$,
\item $A_j-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and the two cycles are not exceptional,
\item $A_j^{2}-B_j$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and only the $\alpha$-cycle is exceptional, 
\item $A_j-B_j^{2}$, if the intersection of an $\alpha$-cycle and a $\beta$-cycle is a vertex $j$ and only the $\beta$-cycle is exceptional,
\item $\gamma_{2}\beta_{b}$, $\beta_{\beta^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1}$, $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{3}$, $\gamma_{3}\gamma_{2}$,
\item $\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}\cdots \alpha_{c}$, $\alpha_{a}\alpha_{b}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1}$, if $u\ne v_2$, 
\\
(We understand that $\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}$, $\alpha_{a}\gamma_{1}$, if $u\ne v_2$ and $b=c=e$),
\item $\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}\cdots \alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}\cdots\alpha_{c}$, 
$\alpha_{a}\alpha_{b}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\alpha_c\alpha_a\alpha_{b}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1}$, if $u=v_2$,
\\ (We understand that $\gamma_{2}\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}$, $\alpha_{a}\alpha_{b}\alpha_{a}\gamma_{1}$, if $u=v_2$ and $b=c=e$),
\item $\alpha_{c}\alpha_{a}-\gamma_{1}\gamma_{2}$,
\item $\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}\alpha_{\alpha(b)}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1}-\gamma_{3}$, if $u\ne v_2$,
\item $(\gamma_{2}\alpha_{b}\alpha_{\alpha(b)}\cdots\alpha_{\alpha^{-1}(c)}\gamma_{1})^{2}-\gamma_{3}$, if $u=v_2$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof for the local algebras $A(\lambda)$
nodes.statement:
Recall that $A(\lambda)=KQ/I$, where 
\[Q=\begin{xy}
(0,0)*[o]+{1}="1",
\SelectTips{eu}{}
\ar @(lu,ld)"1";"1"_{\alpha}
\ar @(ru,rd)"1";"1"^{\beta}
\end{xy}\] 
and $I$ is the admissible ideal generated by $\alpha^{2},$ $\beta^{2},$ $\alpha\beta-\lambda\beta\alpha$.

If $\lambda=1$, then $A(1)$ is cellular. 
Suppose that $A(\lambda)$ is a cellular algebra with cell datum $(\Lambda,\mathcal{T},\mathcal{C},\iota)$. 
Since $\lambda\neq 0$ and $A$ is local, $A(\lambda)$ is the unique indecomposable projective module, and its basis is given by
\[ A(\lambda) = Ke_1\oplus K\alpha \oplus K\beta\oplus K\alpha\beta. \]
Thus, the Cartan matrix of $A(\lambda)$ is $(4)$. 
Let $\mathbf D$ be the decomposition matrix of $A(\lambda)$. 
By (i) and (iii) from Proposition \ref{C Prop decom matrix}, we have 
$\mathbf D=(1\ 1\ 1\ 1)^T$. It implies that $\Lambda=\{\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3, \lambda_4\}$ and 
we may assume without loss of generality that $\lambda_1$ is minimal in the partial order, and we may extend the partial order 
to the total order $1 < 2 < 3 < 4$. The equality $\dim A(\lambda)=\sum_{i=1}^4 |\mathcal{T}(\lambda_i)|^{2}$ implies that we may set
\[ \mathcal{T}(\lambda_1)=\mathcal{T}(\lambda_2)=\mathcal{T}(\lambda_3)=\mathcal{T}(\lambda_4)=\{1\}. \]
The cellular basis is $\mathcal{C}=\{c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1}\ |\ i=1,2,3,4\}$ and $\iota(c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1})=c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1}$
implies that the anti-involution $\iota$ fixes all elements of $A(\lambda)$. It follows that
\[ \alpha\beta=\iota(\alpha\beta)=\iota(\lambda\beta\alpha)=\lambda\iota(\alpha)\iota(\beta)=\lambda\alpha\beta. \]
Therefore, we obtain $\lambda=1$.

nodes.statement_short: All cell modules are one-dimensional, so the anti-involution is the identity, forcing $\alpha\beta=\lambda\alpha\beta$, i.e. $\lambda=1$.

The cellular basis is $\mathcal{C}=\{c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1}\ |\ i=1,2,3,4\}$ and $\iota(c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1})=c^{\lambda_i}_{1,1}$
implies that the anti-involution $\iota$ fixes all elements of $A(\lambda)$. It follows that
\[ \alpha\beta=\iota(\alpha\beta)=\iota(\lambda\beta\alpha)=\lambda\iota(\alpha)\iota(\beta)=\lambda\alpha\beta. \]
Therefore, we obtain $\lambda=1$.

nodes.statement:
We see that the Cartan matrix of $\Lambda'(T)$ is
\[ \mathbf C = \begin{pmatrix}
2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 
1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\

0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 
\end{pmatrix}. \]

the argument there shows that $\Lambda'(T)$ cannot be cellular.

nodes.name: Symmetry $\Lambda'(T(l,m))\cong\Lambda'(T(m,l))$ and five cases
nodes.statement:
We write $\Lambda'(T(l,m))=KQ(l,m)/I$ and recall the generators of the ideal $I$ for the following five cases. 
Then, from those explicit generators, it is easy to see that $\Lambda'(T(l,m))\cong \Lambda'(T(m,l))$, so that the five cases suffice. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] $m\ge l\ge 2$ or $m>l\geq 1$.
\item[(b)] $m=l=1$.
\item[(c)] $l=0$, $m>1$.
\item[(d)] $l=0$, $m=1$.
\item[(e)] $l=m=0$.
\end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
conclusions: $\Lambda'(T(l,m))\cong \Lambda'(T(m,l))$, so that the five cases suffice.

nodes.name: Presentation and projectives of $\Lambda'(T(l,m))$, case (a)
nodes.statement:
Suppose that we are in the case (a). Then $I$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\alpha_i\alpha_{i+1}$, for $-l\leq i\leq -3$ or $1\leq i\leq m-1$ (if $l=1$, then $1\leq i\leq m-1$), 
\item $\beta_i\beta_{i-1}$, for $-l+1\leq i\leq -1$ or $3\leq i\leq m$ (if $l=1$, then $3\leq i\leq m$), 
\item $\alpha_m\beta_m$, $\gamma_0\alpha_1$, $\beta_2\gamma_1$ and $\delta_0\beta_{-1}$,
\item $\beta_{-l}\alpha_{-l}$, $\alpha_{-2}\delta_{-1}$ (if $l=1$, then $\beta_{-1}\delta_{-1}$),
\item $\alpha_i\beta_{i+1}-\beta_i\alpha_{i-1}$, for $-l+1\leq i\leq -2$ or $2\leq i\leq m-1$ (if $l=1$, then $2\leq i\leq m-1$), 
\item $\alpha_m-\beta_m\alpha_{m-1}$ and $\beta_{-l}-\alpha_{-l}\beta_{-l+1}$, (if $l=1$, then $\beta_{-l}-\alpha_{-l}\beta_{-l+1}$ does not occur.)
\item $\alpha_{1}\beta_{2}-\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}$,
\item $\beta_{-1}\alpha_{-2}-\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0$ (if $l=1$, then $\beta_{-1}-\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0$),
\item $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{0}$, $\delta_{-1}\delta_{0}$, $\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}-\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$.
\end{enumerate}
By using (vi) or (viii), we delete the arrows $\alpha_{m}$ and $\beta_{-l}$ from $Q(l,m)$ 
to obtain the Gabriel quiver, 
and replace $\alpha_m$ (respectively, $\beta_{-l}$) in the above generators of $I$ with 
$\beta_m\alpha_{m-1}$ (respectively, $\alpha_{-l}\beta_{-l+1}$ or $\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0$ if $l=1$). 
Explicit computation shows that the indecomposable projective modules are given by
\[\begin{array}{lcl}
P_{-l} &=& Ke_{-l}\oplus K\beta_{-l+1} \oplus K\alpha_{-l}\beta_{-l+1} \;\text{(if $l\ge 2$)}, \\
P_{i} &=& Ke_{i} \oplus  K\alpha_{i-1} \oplus K\beta_{i+1}\oplus K\alpha_{i}\beta_{i+1} \quad (i\notin \{-l, -1,0,1,m\}), \\
P_{-1} &=& \begin{cases}
Ke_{-1}\oplus K\alpha_{-2}\oplus K\delta_{0} \oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}
\oplus K\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\delta_{0} \oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_1\delta_0 \;&\text{(if $l\ge2$)},\\
Ke_{-1}\oplus K\delta_{0} \oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}
\oplus K\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\delta_{0} \oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_1\delta_0 \;&\text{(if $l=1$)},
\end{cases}\\
P_{0} &=& Ke_0\oplus K\delta_{-1}\oplus K\gamma_{1} \oplus K\delta_{0}\delta_{-1} \oplus K\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1} \\
        & & \oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\oplus K\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0\delta_{-1}, \\
P_1  &=& Ke_1\oplus K\beta_2\oplus K\gamma_0\oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\oplus K\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_0\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}, \\
P_m &=& Ke_m\oplus K\alpha_{m-1} \oplus K\beta_m\alpha_{m-1}.     
\end{array} \]
nodes.section: Self-injective cellular algebras of domestic type
nodes.statement_short: Generators of $I$ in case (a), the Gabriel quiver, and bases of the indecomposable projectives.

nodes.name: Presentation and projectives of $\Lambda'(T(1,1))$, case (b)
nodes.statement:
Suppose that we are in the case (b). Then $I$ is the ideal generated by the following elements:
\begin{enumerate}
\item  $\alpha_1\gamma_1$, $\gamma_0\alpha_1$, $\beta_{-1}\delta_{-1}$ and $\delta_0\beta_{-1}$, 
\item $\alpha_{1}-\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}$ and $\beta_{-1}-\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0$,
\item $\gamma_{1}\gamma_{0}$, $\delta_{-1}\delta_{0}$, $\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}-\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}$.
\end{enumerate}
By using (ii), we delete the arrows $\alpha_{1}$ and $\beta_{-1}$ from $Q(1,1)$ to obtain the Gabriel quiver  
and replace $\alpha_1$ (respectively, $\beta_{-1}$) in the above generators of $I$ 
by $\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{1}\gamma_{0}$ (respectively, $\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0$). 
Explicit computation shows 
\[\begin{array}{lcl}
P_{-1} &=&Ke_{-1}\oplus K\delta_{0}\oplus K\gamma_1\delta_{0} \oplus K\gamma_0\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}, \\
P_{0} &=& Ke_0\oplus K\delta_{-1}\oplus K\gamma_{1} \oplus K\delta_{0}\delta_{-1} \oplus K\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_{0}\delta_{-1} \\
        & & \oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}\gamma_{1}\oplus K\gamma_0\gamma_1\delta_0\delta_{-1}, \\
P_1  &=& Ke_1\oplus K\gamma_0\oplus K\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\oplus K\delta_{0}\delta_{-1}\gamma_0\oplus K\gamma_{1}\delta_0\delta_{-1}\gamma_{0}. \\   
\end{array} \]
